editorial.headline: Second-Hand Fashion Retail Is Nationally Open—but Not for PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers retail sales of used clothing, footwear and apparel accessories, with national PMA openness meeting a permanent Bali-wide restriction.
editorial.body:
Second-hand fashion retail is a distinct retail activity: the sale of pre-owned clothing, footwear and clothing accessories. Its practical inventory is familiar—used shirts, trousers, coats, shoes, scarves and hats—but the classification is defined by the retail trade in those used goods, rather than by a particular style, resale channel or customer profile. It gives a clear home to an operator whose business is built around bringing used apparel and related items to market.

The activity is open across the full business-scale range recorded here: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That breadth matters because the classification is not written only for a large-format retail proposition. It accommodates the activity at each of those recognised scales, while keeping the commercial focus precise: used garments, used footwear and used apparel complements sold at retail.

At the national level, the PMA position is straightforward. The activity is TERBUKA, with a maximum foreign ownership level of 100%. In other words, national treatment permits full foreign ownership for this activity. That national openness is grounded in Perpres 10/2021 and 49/2021, and should be read as the national ownership setting—not as a guarantee that every provincial registration environment reaches the same result.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreigner cannot register this activity for PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, OSS assigns low or medium-low risk across every scope, placing the activity within Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. The recorded restriction took effect through the Bali moratorium on 13 May 2026. The contrast is therefore real rather than technical: a 100% national foreign-ownership ceiling does not overcome Bali’s local PMA block for this activity. For a founder assessing the opportunity, the honest conclusion is simple: nationally open, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the stated risk-based moratorium.
